title: Lesson 19: Medical Imaging - Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
Medical imaging (X-rays, CT, MRI) is a leading application of deep learning. CNNs can detect pneumonia, fractures, and tumors, but require large datasets, careful validation, and attention to bias and shortcut learning.


Deep learning transformed medical imaging. Esteva et al. (2017) showed CNNs can match dermatologists in skin-cancer classification, and Rajpurkar et al. (2017) demonstrated radiologist-level pneumonia detection on chest X-rays (CheXNet). Both papers are widely read and include accessible discussions of data, bias, and clinical integration.
Citations: - Esteva A et al. Dermatologist-level classification of skin cancer with deep neural networks. Nature (2017). - Rajpurkar P et al. CheXNet: Radiologist-level pneumonia detection on chest X-rays with deep learning. arXiv (2017).

AI prompts to learn this model

Starter code
import torch
from torchvision import models, transforms
from torchvision.datasets import ImageFolder
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

tfm = transforms.Compose([transforms.Resize((224, 224)),
                          transforms.ToTensor(),
                          transforms.Normalize([0.485, 0.456, 0.406], [0.229, 0.224, 0.225])])
train = ImageFolder("chest_xray/train", transform=tfm)
loader = DataLoader(train, batch_size=32, shuffle=True)
model = models.resnet18(weights="IMAGENET1K_V1")
model.fc = torch.nn.Linear(model.fc.in_features, 2)
print("ready")

title: Lesson 17: Drug Discovery - Random Forest on Molecules
text:
Drug discovery screens thousands of compounds for activity. Molecular descriptors (physicochemical properties) can predict toxicity or activity, accelerating prioritization. Tree-based models handle mixed, high-dimensional descriptors well.


Machine learning accelerates drug discovery by predicting compound activity or toxicity from molecular structure. Svetnik et al. (2003) showed random forests work well for compound classification, and Rogers & Hahn (2010) introduced extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFP) now standard for representing molecules. Both are readable introductions to cheminformatics ML.
Citations: - Svetnik V et al. Random forest: a classification and regression tool for compound classification and QSAR modeling. Journal of Chemical Information and Computer Sciences (2003). - Rogers D, Hahn M. Extended-connectivity fingerprints. Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling (2010).

Starter code
import pandas as pd
from rdkit import Chem
from rdkit.Chem import Descriptors
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

df = pd.read_csv("tox21.csv")
def feats(smi):
    m = Chem.MolFromSmiles(smi)
    return [Descriptors.MolWt(m), Descriptors.MolLogP(m), Descriptors.TPSA(m)]
X = df["smiles"].apply(feats).tolist()
y = df["NR-AR"]
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=42)
print("CV AUC:", cross_val_score(rf, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean())

“How do I avoid data leakage across similar molecules (scaffold split)?”
“Why is AUC-PR more informative than AUC-ROC for rare toxicity?”

title: Lesson 15: Wearables - Physical Activity Recognition from Accelerometers
text:
Wearable devices (smartwatches, fitness trackers, smartphones) continuously record movement, heart rate, and sleep. These data enable large-scale studies of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep patterns. A common task is activity recognition: classifying what a person is doing (walking, sitting, climbing stairs) from raw accelerometer signals. This requires turning time-series into features and handling person-to-person variability.


Wearable-based activity recognition has matured from lab studies to free-living populations. Bao and Intille (2004) showed that simple accelerometers with machine learning can recognize daily activities. Troiano et al. (2008) used accelerometer data in NHANES to characterize US physical activity levels, a landmark population study. These papers are approachable and show both method and public-health impact.
Citations: - Bao L, Intille SS. Activity recognition from user-annotated acceleration data. Pervasive Computing (2004). - Troiano RP et al. Physical activity in the United States measured by accelerometer. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise (2008). - Kwapisz JR, Weiss GM, Moore SA. Activity recognition using cell phone accelerometers. SIGKDD Explorations (2011) (WISDM dataset).

title: Lesson 13: Causal Inference - Propensity Scores (NHANES)
text:
Observational health studies are plagued by confounding. Causal inference methods (propensity scores, matching, weighting) aim to estimate treatment effects as if from a randomized trial. NHANES provides rich, nationally representative health data.


Observational studies dominate health research, but confounding threatens causal claims. Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983) introduced the propensity score as a way to balance confounders, and Austin (2011) provides an accessible introduction to propensity-score methods for applied researchers. NHANES is a widely used, nationally representative data source for such analyses.
Citations: - Rosenbaum PR, Rubin DB. The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects. Biometrika (1983). - Austin PC. An introduction to propensity score methods for reducing the effects of confounding in observational studies. Multivariate Behavioral Research (2011).

AI prompts to learn this model

“Explain propensity scores and how they balance confounders in observational studies.”
“What are the key assumptions for causal inference (positivity, no unmeasured confounding)?”



Starter code
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
import numpy as np

df = pd.read_csv("nhanes.csv")  # columns: smoke (0/1), age, sex, bmi, sbp, ...
conf = ["age", "sex", "bmi"]
ps_model = LogisticRegression().fit(df[conf], df["smoke"])
df["ps"] = ps_model.predict_proba(df[conf])[:, 1]
# Nearest-neighbor matching on logit(ps)
logit = np.log(df["ps"]/(1-df["ps"]))
# ... match treated to control
print(df.groupby("smoke")["sbp"].mean())


Suggested AI prompts

“What is a propensity score and what does it balance?”
“How do I check covariate balance after matching?”
“What assumptions (positivity, no unmeasured confounding) are required?”



Extensions

title: Lesson 11: Anomaly Detection - Isolation Forest

Anomalies in health data can indicate fraud, rare diseases, sensor errors, or outbreaks. Unsupervised anomaly detection flags unusual cases without labels, useful when labeled anomalies are scarce.

title: Lesson 9: Mental Health Text - Naive Bayes and NLP
text:
Mental health conditions are often first expressed in language. Analyzing text from forums, surveys, or clinical notes can support screening and triage, but raises serious privacy and ethics concerns. Naive Bayes remains a strong, interpretable baseline for text classification.


Language is a window into mental health. De Choudhury et al. (2013) showed that social media language can predict depression, sparking a large literature on digital mental health. Naive Bayes, despite its strong independence assumptions, remains a fast and interpretable baseline for text classification (Pang & Lee 2008). These works are accessible and highlight both promise and ethical pitfalls.
Citations: - De Choudhury M et al. Predicting depression via social media. ICWSM (2013). - Pang B, Lee L. Opinion mining and sentiment analysis. Foundations and Trends in Information Retrieval (2008).

Starter code
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

df = pd.read_csv("mental_health_posts.csv")  # columns: text, label
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(df["text"], df["label"],
                                       test_size=0.2, stratify=df["label"], random_state=42)
pipe = Pipeline([("tfidf", TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", max_features=5000)),
                 ("nb", MultinomialNB())])
pipe.fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(classification_report(yte, pipe.predict(Xte)))

“Why is Naive Bayes ‘naive’, and why does it still work for text?”
“How do I inspect which words drive each class prediction?”
“What are the ethical risks of classifying mental health from social media?”

title: Lesson 7: Hospital Readmission - Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
text:
Unplanned hospital readmissions are costly and often preventable. Predicting which patients will return within 30 days lets hospitals target discharge planning and follow-up. The data is messy: mixed types, missingness, and rare outcomes.


Hospital readmissions are a major quality and cost issue. Kansagara et al. (2011) systematically reviewed readmission risk models and found most had modest discrimination, highlighting the difficulty of the problem. Gradient boosting (Friedman 2001) and its efficient implementation XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin 2016) became standard tools for tabular clinical data. Read these for a realistic sense of both the clinical challenge and the method.
Citations: - Kansagara D et al. Risk prediction models for hospital readmission. JAMA (2011). - Chen T, Guestrin C. XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System. KDD (2016).

title: Lesson 3: Train/Test Splitting and Honest Evaluation
text:
A model that memorizes the data it was trained on is useless in practice. Train/test splitting is the simplest way to estimate how a model will perform on new patients. Done wrong (leakage, imbalance, no stratification), it gives misleading optimism. This lesson is methodological but uses a health dataset.


How we evaluate a model matters as much as the model itself. Kohavi (1995) compared cross-validation and bootstrap for accuracy estimation and showed that stratified 10-fold CV is a strong default. Raschka (2018) provides an accessible modern treatment of model evaluation, including leakage and nested CV. The lesson here is methodological: an honest split is the foundation of trustworthy ML in health.
Citations: - Kohavi R. A study of cross-validation and bootstrap for accuracy estimation and model selection. IJCAI (1995). - Raschka S. Model evaluation, model selection, and algorithm selection in machine learning. arXiv (2018).

title: Lesson 1: Predicting Birth Weight - Linear Regression
text:
Birth weight is a key indicator of newborn health; low birth weight is linked to infant mortality and developmental problems. Maternal factors (age, weight, smoking, hypertension, etc.) are associated with birth weight. Linear regression gives an interpretable baseline: each coefficient estimates the change in expected birth weight per unit change in a predictor.


Predicting birth weight from maternal characteristics is a classic problem in perinatal epidemiology. Kramer (1987) synthesized decades of work showing that maternal nutrition, smoking, and hypertension are among the strongest determinants of low birth weight. Wilcox (2001) reminds us that birth weight is a proxy, not a cause—models should be interpreted carefully and not over-interpreted as causal. For an accessible overview, see Wilcox, On the importance—and the unimportance—of birthweight, International Journal of Epidemiology (2001).
Citations: - Kramer MS. Determinants of low birth weight: methodological assessment and meta-analysis. Bulletin of the World Health Organization (1987). - Wilcox AJ. On the importance—and the unimportance—of birthweight. International Journal of Epidemiology (2001).

title: Lesson 2: Cardiovascular Disease Risk - Logistic Regression
text:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide. Risk factors such as age, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, and diabetes are well established, and clinicians routinely combine them into risk scores (e.g., the Framingham Risk Score). Machine learning can reproduce and extend these scores, but interpretability matters: a model that a physician cannot explain will not be adopted.


The Framingham Heart Study, begun in 1948, established the major cardiovascular risk factors (age, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, diabetes) that clinicians still use. Wilson et al. (1998) turned these into the familiar risk-factor categories, and D’Agostino et al. (2008) produced the general CVD risk profile used in primary care. These papers are approachable and show how simple logistic models can guide clinical decisions.
Citations: - Wilson PWF et al. Prediction of coronary heart disease using risk factor categories. Circulation (1998). - D’Agostino RB et al. General cardiovascular risk profile for use in primary care. Circulation (2008).

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, classification_report
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

df = pd.read_csv("framingham.csv")
X = df.drop(columns=["TenYearCHD"])
y = df["TenYearCHD"]
X = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(X)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced")
model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
proba = model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
print("AUC:", roc_auc_score(yte, proba))
print(classification_report(yte, (proba > 0.5).astype(int)))

Healthcare spending is right-skewed and heteroscedastic: a few patients dominate costs. Generalized linear models (GLMs) with appropriate families (Gamma, Tweedie) and link functions model such outcomes better than ordinary least squares.


Healthcare spending is right-skewed and heteroscedastic, making ordinary least squares a poor fit. Manning and Mullahy (2001) compare estimators for log-models of medical expenditures, and Diehr et al. (1999) review methods for analyzing healthcare utilization and cost. These papers motivate GLMs with Gamma or Tweedie families.
Citations: - Manning WG, Mullahy J. Estimating log models: to transform or not to transform? Journal of Health Economics (2001). - Diehr P et al. Methods for analyzing health care utilization and costs. Annual Review of Public Health (1999).

title: Lesson 16: Gut Microbiome - Compositional Data and Classification
text:
The human gut microbiome comprises trillions of microbes that influence digestion, immunity, and disease. Researchers profile microbiomes by sequencing (16S rRNA or metagenomics), producing tables of taxa abundances. These data are compositional (relative abundances summing to 1), sparse, and high-dimensional. ML can classify disease states from microbiome profiles, but requires care with compositionality and batch effects.


Microbiome research expanded rapidly with sequencing. Turnbaugh et al. (2009) linked gut microbiome composition to obesity, and the Human Microbiome Project (2012) characterized healthy microbiomes. Compositional data analysis (Gloor et al. 2017) warns that standard methods can mislead on relative-abundance data. These are accessible entry points.
Citations: - Turnbaugh PJ et al. A core gut microbiome in obese and lean twins. Nature (2009). - Human Microbiome Project Consortium. Structure, function and diversity of the healthy human microbiome. Nature (2012). - Gloor GB et al. Microbiome datasets are compositional: and this is not optional. Frontiers in Microbiology (2017).

title: Lesson 18: Clinical Notes (EHR) - Transformers / BERT
text:
Clinical notes contain rich information not captured in structured fields. NLP can extract phenotypes, predict outcomes, and support coding. Transformers (BERT) dominate, but clinical variants (ClinicalBERT, BioBERT) and privacy constraints matter.


Clinical notes contain rich information not captured in structured data. Alsentzer et al. (2019) released clinical BERT embeddings trained on MIMIC notes, and Devlin et al. (2019) introduced BERT. These works show how transfer learning can unlock clinical text, while raising privacy and fairness concerns.
Citations: - Alsentzer E et al. Publicly available clinical BERT embeddings. ClinicalNLP Workshop (2019). - Devlin J et al. BERT: Pre-training of deep bidirectional transformers for language understanding. NAACL (2019).
